---

## 1. Exact compact-WY / blocked Householder math (matches LAPACK dgeqrf)

Sources: Reference-LAPACK `master` source — `dlarft.f`, `dlarfb.f`, `dlarfg.f`, `dgeqr2.f`, `dgeqrf.f`, `dlarf1f.f`, `ilaenv.f` (raw URLs at end of section); Schreiber–Van Loan 1989 (https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/0910005).

**Single reflector**: `H_i = I − tau_i v_i v_iᵀ`. LAPACK folds normalization into tau — it is **NOT** `2vvᵀ/(vᵀv)`. (Confirmed in `dlarf1f.f`.)

**Block reflector**: `Q = H₁H₂…H_k = I − V T Vᵀ` — **no transpose on the first V**. V is unit-lower-trapezoidal columnwise. T is **upper-triangular k×k with tau on the diagonal**.

### 1a. Forming T (DLARFT, DIRECT='F', STOREV='C')

Your recalled recurrence is **correct**. Column by column, for j = 1..k:

```
if tau_j == 0:  T(1:j, j) = 0
else:
    w            = V(:,1:j-1)ᵀ @ V(:,j)            # length j-1; V has unit diag
    T(1:j-1, j)  = T(1:j-1,1:j-1) @ ( -tau_j * w ) # one minus sign, on tau_j
    T(j, j)      = tau_j
```

LAPACK computes `−tau_j·w` first (steps A+B: a DGEMV) then left-multiplies by the existing `T(1:j-1,1:j-1)` (step C: a DTRMV). Since `T_block @ (−tau_j w) = −tau_j T_block @ w`, your single-expression form is algebraically identical. **One minus sign, on tau_j, applied to the full inner product.** (`dlarft.f`.) Note: current LAPACK `master` ships a *recursive* DLARFT that computes the same T via `T₁₂ = −T₁₁(V₁ᵀV₂)T₂₂`; the classic column loop above is simpler to reproduce and bit-compatible with the definition.

### 1b. The LEFT trailing update — it is **T-transpose** (DLARFB, SIDE='L', TRANS='T')

QR produces R by applying `Qᵀ = (I − VTVᵀ)ᵀ = I − V Tᵀ Vᵀ` from the left. So the trailing update operator is **`C := (I − V Tᵀ Vᵀ) C`** — transpose on T. In the natural `W = VᵀC` layout, the three steps are:

```
W = Vᵀ @ C        # K×N_trail; V unit-lower-trapezoidal (implicit 1 diag)
W = Tᵀ @ W        # T upper-tri  ->  Tᵀ lower-tri
C = C − V @ W      # rank-k downdate
```

This is the form to implement. (A subtlety worth flagging so you don't get misled reading LAPACK directly: `dlarfb.f` stores its workspace *transposed* as `W=CᵀV` and therefore calls DTRMM with op(T)=**'N'** when TRANS='T'. That 'N' is *not* a contradiction — the transpose has moved onto the workspace orientation. The math applied is unambiguously `I − V Tᵀ Vᵀ`. dgeqrf calls dlarfb with `'Left','Transpose'`, confirming it.)

### 1c. Single reflector generation (DLARFG) — exact, including rank deficiency

Given column `x = [alpha; x_tail]`, `xnorm = ||x_tail||₂`:

```
if xnorm == 0:                 # tail below diagonal is exactly zero (rank-deficient / already triangular)
    tau = 0;  v unused;  beta = alpha     # H = I, no reflection
else:
    beta = -sign(alpha) * sqrt(alpha² + xnorm²)   # full norm incl. alpha; -sign avoids cancellation
    tau  = (beta - alpha) / beta                  # lands in [1,2]
    v(1) = 1 (implicit);  v(2:) = x_tail / (alpha - beta)
    # R diagonal entry = beta
```

This confirms all your formulas. **Rank-deficiency handling**: the condition is `xnorm == 0` → `tau=0`, reflector skipped. I observed exactly this (`tau=0.0`) from torch.geqrf on a singular column. LAPACK additionally does **safe-scaling**: if `|beta| < SAFMIN` it scales `x_tail, alpha, beta` up by `1/SAFMIN` (≤20×), recomputes the norm, then deflates beta back — guards underflow/overflow in the norm. The robust `sqrt(a²+b²)` is `dlapy2`: `w=max(|a|,|b|); z=min; w·sqrt(1+(z/w)²)`.

### 1d. dgeqrf loop & block size

```
for i in 1..K step nb:
    ib = min(K-i+1, nb)
    DGEQR2(panel A[i:m, i:i+ib])     # unblocked: v's + tau (the SERIAL part)
    DLARFT(...)                       # form T (ib×ib)
    DLARFB('Left','Transpose',...)    # trailing update A[i:m, i+ib:n]  (the GEMM part)
```

## 2. torch.geqrf packing & householder_product (verified on B200)

Covered above in §0. Key points restated for clarity: column-major-equivalent storage doesn't matter to you because torch hands you a row-major contiguous tensor and `triu`/`tril` index it directly. The unit diagonal on V is **implicit** — you write only the strictly-below-diagonal v entries into H; `householder_product` supplies the 1's. `tau` is `(batch, n)` and indexed per reflector. Producing `tau=0` for a degenerate column is both legal and what LAPACK does; `householder_product` treats that reflector as identity. Docs: https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.geqrf.html and https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.linalg.householder_product.html.

---

## 3. Fast GPU implementations to emulate

**MAGMA batched geqrf — the canonical structural template.** `magma_sgeqrf_batched` → host loop over panels stepping by `nb`, in lockstep across the whole batch: `geqrf_panel_batched` → `slarft_batched` (form T) → `slarfb_gemm_batched` (trailing update = **three array-of-pointers batched GEMMs**: `W=VᵀC`, `W2=TW`, `C=C−VW2`). The sequential dependency is the host panel loop; the batch is pure data-parallelism per wave (`ceil(min(m,n)/nb)` waves regardless of batch size). **nb=32, hard-coded**, with two-level nesting **32 → 8-wide sub-panel → unblocked geqr2**; the innermost serial loop is the per-column geqr2 step. Caveat for your leaderboard: MAGMA has a 10-stream per-matrix fallback for larger shapes that uses **non-default CUDA streams + host pointer arithmetic — your harness rejects that** (your `leaderboard-default-stream-only` memory). Only the batched-GEMM path maps cleanly.

Time breakdown at 256×256: geqr2 ~30%, GEMM ~56% (panel dominates as size shrinks); and a **register-cached fully-unrolled geqr2 for n≤32 that skips T and the batched GEMM entirely**, beating cuBLAS/KBLAS up to 3.22×. PDF: https://www.netlib.org/utk/people/JackDongarra/PAPERS/batchqr-gpu-2022.pdf

**cuSOLVER / "domino" — two corrections.** (a) cuSOLVER has **no batched dense Householder QR** — its batched dense routines are Cholesky/Jacobi-SVD/eig only. The only NVIDIA batched dense QR is `cublas<t>geqrfBatched` (small-matrix, and it has no batched orgqr/ormqr partner). (b) The **"domino" scheme is sparse**, not dense QR — it's Lung-Sheng Chien's global-sync-avoidance for sparse triangular solve / sparse QR (GTC 2014), productized in cuSolverRF sparse LU refactorization. There is **no public NVIDIA "domino" dense-QR algorithm**; if you had that in mind for dense QR it doesn't map to a documented method. The most relevant NVIDIA-native primitive is **cuSOLVERDx `geqrf`** — a device-function QR you embed in your own kernel, one matrix per CTA/warp-group, no launch overhead (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cusolverdx/get_started/functions/geqrf.html); internals undocumented beyond "Householder reflections." Sparse-batched-QR blog (for context only): https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/parallel-direct-solvers-with-cusolver-batched-qr/

**TSQR / CAQR — the natural panel factorization.** A square matrix factored panel-by-panel has *tall-skinny* panels, so TSQR is the right on-chip panel method: split panel into row blocks, independent local Householder QR per block (leaves, no sync), then merge by **stacking two n×n R's into 2n×n and re-factoring** up a reduction tree. Critical-path length is tree depth (`log P`), replacing the `n` global BLAS-2 syncs of standard Householder QR with one on-chip reduction. GPU mapping (Anderson/Ballard/Demmel/Keutzer, IPDPS 2011): four kernels (`factor`, `factor_tree`, `apply_qt_h`, `apply_qt_tree`), **one thread-block per small-block QR, 64 threads/block, 64×16 blocks → quad-tree**, block kept **entirely in registers** with cyclic column distribution (85 → 248 GFLOPS). Foundational CAQR: Demmel/Grigori/Hoemmen/Langou, LAWN 204, https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lawnspdf/lawn204.pdf · GPU CAQR: http://www.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2010/EECS-2010-131.pdf · CUDA/TensorCore TSQR code: https://github.com/enp1s0/tsqr-gpu · batched TSQR: https://github.com/ecrc/kblas-gpu

**CUTLASS (backs the trailing GEMM; no factorization examples).** For B200 the key example is **`75_blackwell_grouped_gemm`** — SM100 TensorOp + TMA warp-specialized grouped GEMM with device-side scheduling, ideal if your trailing sub-blocks have non-uniform shapes: https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/examples/75_blackwell_grouped_gemm/75_blackwell_grouped_gemm.cu . **Triton linear algebra — genuinely sparse.** No general QR/LU/Cholesky Triton library exists. The single most relevant artifact is **`nshejwalkar/linalg-gpu-comp`** (https://github.com/nshejwalkar/linalg-gpu-comp) — an agent-driven run on **this exact `qr_v2` B200 problem** (~24 submissions + notes). Its findings, which you should treat as a map of the terrain:
  - Panel is the bottleneck (~31–40% of GPU time), explicitly *"sequential/reduction-bound — inherent to Householder, not fixable by precision or GEMM tricks."*

**Tensor-core / mixed-precision QR (2023–2025) — the B200 lever.** Most relevant: **Leng et al., "High-Performance Householder QR on Emerging GPU Architectures Using Tensor Cores," IEEE TPDS 36(3), Mar 2025** — switches Gram-Schmidt→Householder/compact-WY to fix orthogonality while keeping TC speed, uses **recursive QR to square-ify the inner GEMMs** (tall-skinny GEMMs waste tensor cores), and emulated precision inside the factorization. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10816084/ . Rounding theory: block/WY Householder is **more** robust in mixed precision than unblocked, and FP16-input/FP32-accumulate inner products are essentially exact (Yang/Fox/Sanders, https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.06217). **Two caveats for your small-square regime**: (1) Thies & Röhrig-Zöllner (benchmarked on B100/B200) — tall-skinny/TSQR is **memory-bound and gets nothing from tensor cores**; when launch/bandwidth-bound, emulated-GEMM tricks buy nothing (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20889). (2) Emulated precision is conditioning-sensitive — validate on your *actual* mixed/ill-conditioned distribution, not random matrices.

---

## 4. Numerics: what breaks, and can you use TF32?

**Householder QR is unconditionally backward stable** — `||A − Q̃R̃|| / ||A|| = O(eps)` and `||Q̃ᵀQ̃ − I|| = O(eps)` regardless of conditioning, *as long as the reflectors are computed and applied in honest precision*. This is exactly why your checker can demand both invariants. Your stress cases map to specific risks:

- **rankdef / nearrank** (zero or near-zero panel columns): the reflector with `xnorm≈0` gives `tau→0`; LAPACK sets `tau=0` exactly and skips it (verified). You must replicate the `xnorm==0 → tau=0` branch, and use the robust `dlapy2` norm + safe-scaling so a tiny-but-nonzero tail doesn't blow up `v = x_tail/(alpha−beta)`. **Backward stability still holds** for rank-deficient A under Householder (R just has tiny/zero diagonal entries); the factor residual gate is against `triu(H)`, so as long as `R=triu(H)` and Q are mutually consistent you pass — you do **not** need rank-revealing pivoting (and pivoting would break the `geqrf` no-pivot contract anyway).
- **clustered / rowscale / cond knob** (wide dynamic range across columns/rows, scales down to `4·eps32` and `sqrt(eps32)`): the danger is **catastrophic cancellation in the norm and in `alpha−beta`**. The `−sign(alpha)` choice of beta and `dlapy2` are precisely the LAPACK guards; keep them. Tiny columns produce tiny R diagonals — fine for the residual (measured relative to `||A||₁`).
- **nearcollinear** (rank-1 + 1e-4 noise): extreme ill-conditioning but full-rank; Householder handles it stably. The trailing columns have small norms after early reflectors — again a cancellation/scaling concern, not a stability one.
- **band / upper**: benign for QR.

**Precision split — this is the key answer:**

- **The panel factorization must be FP32 (honest), not TF32.** Norms, beta, tau, and the v-scaling `x_tail/(alpha−beta)` are cancellation-prone; doing them in ~10-bit TF32 will violate the orthogonality gate on the ill-conditioned cases. Compute the panel reductions and reflector arithmetic in FP32 (FMA/CUDA-core math, `tl.sum`, etc.). The competitor on this exact problem found the same.
- **The trailing GEMM update can use TF32 tensor cores — with care.** The update `C −= V(Tᵀ(VᵀC))` accumulates in FP32. A single-pass `"tf32"` (10-bit inputs) is **risky** on the wide-dynamic-range cases (clustered/rowscale/cond=4) and can fail orthogonality; the truncation-not-rounding bias makes it worse. The safe, fast choice is **3xTF32 / `input_precision="tf32x3"`** (Triton) or **BF16x9** (cuBLAS on Blackwell) — both recover **≥ FP32-class accuracy** at ~3× / ~9× the tensor-core FLOPs, which still beats native FP32 on B200 because peak TF32/BF16 throughput ≫ 9× peak FP32. Your tolerance at n=512 is ~1.2e-3 relative, which is *loose* — single-pass TF32 will pass the well-conditioned majority easily, so a viable strategy is: **TF32 trailing update by default, validated on the mixed/ill-conditioned benchmark shapes**; fall back to tf32x3 only if a shape fails. But note the benchmark set deliberately includes `mixed`, `rankdef`, `clustered`, `nearrank` *as ranked cases*, so the accurate path's cost is part of your score — you can't route everything to a fast-but-invalid path.
- A cheap insurance policy if orthogonality is marginal: **one re-orthogonalization / iterative-refinement pass** on Q after a TF32 update (Higham–Mary mixed-precision survey, https://hal.science/hal-03537373v2).

## 5. Triton specifics (verified: Triton 3.6.0 on this box — well past the sm_100 threshold)

**tl.dot precision** (`input_precision=`): NVIDIA accepts `"tf32"`, `"tf32x3"`, `"ieee"` (the MLIR layer also has `"bf16x3"`/`"bf16x6"`). Default for FP32 inputs on tensor-core GPUs is **`"tf32"`**; override globally with env `TRITON_F32_DEFAULT`. `allow_tf32` is deprecated (`True`≡`"tf32"`, `False`≡`"ieee"`).
- `"tf32"`: single TF32 MMA, 10-bit-mantissa inputs, FP32 accumulate. Fast; may *truncate* (bias) — round to TF32 yourself or load via `TensorDescriptor(round_f32_to_tf32=True)` (issue #4574).
- `"tf32x3"`: the 3xTF32 trick — split each FP32 into hi/lo TF32, do `aBig·bBig + aSmall·bBig + aBig·bSmall` (drops lo·lo, zeros inf·0 NaNs). **~21–22 effective mantissa bits ≈ near-FP32**, ~3× a TF32 dot. This is the sweet spot for FP32-accuracy GEMM in Triton. Source: https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/main/lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/F32DotTC.cpp
- `"ieee"`: true FP32 on FMA/CUDA cores (not tensor cores) — bit-accurate, much slower.
- **There is no native FP32-input tensor-core MMA on Blackwell** — FP32 inputs are always TF32-reduced, emulated (tf32x3/bf16xN), or run on FMA cores. Accumulator is FP32 regardless.

```python
acc = tl.zeros((BM, BN), tl.float32)
acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc, input_precision="tf32x3")   # near-FP32, tensor cores
```

**Accumulator**: FP32 by default; thread an explicit `tl.zeros(..., tl.float32)` through your K-loop. **Blackwell**: Triton 3.6 emits **`tcgen05.mma` (5th-gen TC via TMEM)** for `tl.dot` on sm_100; support landed in Triton 3.3 / PyTorch 2.7, so your 3.6/2.11 stack is mature. Docs: https://triton-lang.org/main/python-api/generated/triton.language.dot.html · MLIR `inputPrecision`: https://triton-lang.org/main/dialects/TritonOps.html

**Panel factorization in Triton — the nuance**: a sequential per-column Householder loop in a *single program mapping one matrix* is a poor fit (serial chain of length b, tiny latency-bound reductions, no grid parallelism along the loop). **But the same loop replicated across the batch grid is acceptable** — assign **one program per batch matrix** and loop over b columns internally; the grid (hundreds of matrices) keeps the GPU busy despite each program's serial inner loop. That is the one regime where a sequential Triton inner loop pays off here, and it's essentially what the competitor's resident-tile B=32 panel does. For n≥512 a wide panel won't fit smem (256 KB > 228 KB), forcing B≤32 or a hand-written CUDA/nvrtc panel.

**Trailing update — torch.bmm vs hand Triton (the practical call):** **Start with `torch.bmm`/`torch.matmul`** for the three products. At 512×512 in batches of hundreds, cuBLAS strided/grouped batched GEMM is NVIDIA-tuned for exactly this regime and uses TF32 tensor cores when enabled; published "beat-cuBLAS" Triton results are for *huge single* GEMMs (M=N=K≈8192), not batches of medium matrices. **Hand-write Triton only if profiling shows the trailing update is HBM-bandwidth-bound on the intermediates** (it often is at 512×512) — then a *single fused* grouped kernel computing `VᵀC → Tᵀ(·) → V(·) →` subtract in one pass, avoiding three HBM round-trips, can win, using `input_precision="tf32x3"` for accuracy. For an isolated `bmm`, cuBLAS is the default.

**Enable TF32 in PyTorch**: `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True` or `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")`. Mapping: `"highest"`(default)=true FP32 (24-bit); `"high"`=TF32 *or* bf16x3 (~16-bit), ≡ `allow_tf32=True`; `"medium"`=bf16. **This only affects cuBLAS/aten — not your Triton `tl.dot`**, whose precision you set separately via `input_precision`. Docs: https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html · https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.set_float32_matmul_precision.html
